sections.title: Safety Principles
items: Always warm up — never skip it even when short on time
Increase load gradually — no more than 10% per week
Rest when you feel pain (pain ≠ discomfort) — listen to your body
Don't train when feverish, acutely injured, or exhausted
Stop immediately if chest pain, dizziness, or shortness of breath

sections.title: Technique & Common Errors

Push: sagging back, neck strain → 'Body like a plank — long neck — push the floor away'
Pull: shrugging shoulders, hunching → 'Pull elbows back — gentle squeeze — ears away from shoulders'
Core: holding breath, arched back → 'Light belly draw — breathe steadily — neutral spine'
Breath: chest breathing vs diaphragm → 'Belly expands on inhale — slow exhale through mouth'

Step 3: Increase difficulty — Sit-to-Stand → Squat → Goblet Squat
Step 4: Add weight or resistance band

warmup.how: Hand on belly, inhale to expand belly gently, exhale slowly through mouth
Walk in place, raise knees moderately, shoulders relaxed
Roll shoulders backward gently, don't hunch neck
Gently draw shoulder blades back, open chest
Push hips back, spine neutral, knees slightly soft
Sit to chair and stand back up, controlling knees

cooldown.how: Kneel one leg, gently push hip forward
Extend one leg, fold gently forward, keep back neutral
Arms behind back or hands on doorframe, open chest

movements_detail.name: Squat
movements_detail.goal: Build quad, glute and knee strength; improve ability to stand/sit; support daily activities.
movements_detail.basic_how: Sit on a chair, feet hip-width apart. Lean slightly forward, push feet into floor to stand. Lower back down slowly — don't drop.
movements_detail.cue: Knees track toes · Heels planted · Chest open

levels.label: Advanced
levels.exercise: Goblet Squat or Tempo Squat (3s down)

movements_detail.errors: Knees caving in, heels lifting, rounding back, going too deep before ready

movements_detail.name: Hinge
movements_detail.goal: Learn proper hip hinge; protect the lower back when bending; train glutes and hamstrings.
movements_detail.basic_how: Stand upright, hands on hips. Soft knees, push hips back as if reaching for a wall behind. Keep spine neutral. When you feel a gentle hamstring pull, stand back up.
movements_detail.cue: Push hips back · Long spine · Light core brace

levels.label: Beginner
levels.exercise: Hip Hinge with hands on hips

movements_detail.errors: Bending at spine instead of hips, rounding back, locking knees, neck hyperextension

movements_detail.name: Push
movements_detail.goal: Build upper body pushing strength; improve ability to push doors, lift objects overhead.
movements_detail.basic_how: Stand an arm's length from wall, hands at chest height. Bend elbows to bring chest toward wall, then push back. Keep body in a straight line — no sagging.
movements_detail.cue: Body like a plank · Long neck · Push the floor/wall away
movements_detail.errors: Sagging back, craning neck, elbows flaring wide, only moving head not torso

movements_detail.name: Pull
movements_detail.goal: Balance push muscles; improve rounded shoulder posture; strengthen upper back.
movements_detail.basic_how: Anchor a band or towel at chest height. Grip both ends, pull elbows back, gently squeeze shoulder blades. Release slowly. Chest open, shoulders away from ears.
movements_detail.cue: Pull elbows back · Gentle shoulder squeeze · Ears away from shoulders

levels.label: Advanced
levels.exercise: One-arm Dumbbell Row or heavier Band Row

movements_detail.errors: Shrugging shoulders, rounding back, pulling with wrists instead of back, releasing too fast

movements_detail.name: Core
movements_detail.goal: Improve trunk stability; support the lower back; correct posture.
movements_detail.basic_how: Lie on back, arms reaching up, knees at 90°. Gently brace core so lower back doesn't arch. Slowly extend opposite arm and leg, then switch.
movements_detail.cue: Gentle belly draw · Breathe steadily · Neutral spine

levels.label: Standard
levels.exercise: Short Plank, Side Plank on knees

movements_detail.errors: Holding breath, arching lower back, hips too high in plank, neck tension

movements_detail.name: Breath
movements_detail.goal: Stabilize the trunk during exercise; reduce stress; support recovery.
movements_detail.basic_how: One hand on chest, one on belly. Inhale through nose to expand belly (not chest), exhale slowly through mouth.
movements_detail.cue: Belly expands on inhale · Slow exhale · Chest relaxed

levels.label: Advanced
levels.exercise: Box Breathing: inhale 4s — hold 4s — exhale 4s — hold 4s

movements_detail.errors: Chest breathing instead of belly, breath-holding during exercise, breathing too fast

pillarA.intro_pt1: Effective training is not about training
pillarA.intro_sub: The 4 topics below are arranged in logical order: from fundamental technique, building training structure, organizing weekly rhythm, to measuring and adjusting progress. Each step prepares for the next.

principles.title: Technique is the foundation
principles.body: Learning correctly from the start saves years of wrong training. 6 fundamental movement patterns cover 95% of all exercises you'll ever need — no complex equipment required.

principles.title: Consistency beats intensity
principles.body: The brain builds habits through regular repetition. 3 sessions/week for 12 weeks beats 7 sessions/week then burnout after 3 — the body needs time to adapt.

principles.title: Measure to stay on track
principles.body: Progress that can't be seen leads to discouragement. Clear milestones every 4 weeks tell you exactly where you are and what to adjust next.

tabs.title: 6 Fundamental Movement Patterns
tabs.longDesc: Learn 6 fundamental movement patterns — the foundation of every effective training program. Each exercise includes a detailed video guide, from correct form to advanced variations. Combined with a 5–8 min warm-up and post-workout cool-down, you get a complete and safe session.

highlights.title: HD video per exercise
highlights.desc: See the angle, technique and correct movement cues clearly

highlights.title: 3 levels per exercise
highlights.desc: From beginner to advanced — clear progressive steps

highlights.title: Science-based warm-up
highlights.desc: Reduces injury risk and improves performance by 15–20%

tabs.quote: Master 6 fundamental movement patterns — and you have the foundation for 95% of every exercise you'll ever need.

details.title: Why only 6 patterns?
details.body: Biomechanists analyzed thousands of exercises and found they are all variations of 6 fundamental patterns. Master the 6 = a permanent foundation for any program.

details.title: Unlimited variations
details.body: Each pattern has 5–10+ variations from super easy to advanced. Chair squat → Pistol squat. No equipment needed — correct form is everything.

details.title: Full-body balance
details.body: Push + Pull balance front/back muscles. Squat + Hinge develop the full lower body. Core stabilizes the spine. Breath controls the whole system — this is the perfect loop.

tabs.title: Daily Training Framework 20–40 Min
tabs.longDesc: Sessions don't need to be long — they need the right structure. 4 time blocks (Warm-Up → Main Workout → Cool-Down → Mind Reset) allow purposeful training in any duration. Choose your window — every minute has a clear plan.

highlights.title: 8 levels: 20–180 min
highlights.desc: From super busy to intensive — all scheduled

highlights.title: Minute-by-minute detail
highlights.desc: Know exactly what to do in each time slot

tabs.quote: Good structure matters more than long duration. 20 planned minutes is more effective than 1 unstructured hour.

details.title: The brain needs structure
details.body: Reducing decisions during a session helps focus on movement quality, not 'what to do next.' Clear structure = less burnout and more consistency over time.

details.title: 4 blocks — one universal structure
details.body: Warm-Up → Main Workout → Cool-Down → Mind Reset. A 20-min or 180-min session uses the same structure — only the time ratio between blocks changes.

details.title: 5-min mind reset — not a luxury
details.body: 5 minutes of controlled breathing post-workout reduces cortisol by 15% and improves nighttime sleep. Smallest investment with the biggest recovery benefit.

tabs.title: Suggested Weekly Rhythm
tabs.longDesc: Fitness is built over weeks, not days. 3 phases of weekly rhythm (Start → Build → Advance) help the body adapt step by step without burnout. 6 goal-based programs help you choose the right rhythm for your specific situation.

highlights.title: 6 goal-based programs
highlights.desc: From super busy to advanced athlete

tabs.quote: The body develops during rest — not during training. Weekly rhythm is the art of knowing when to stop.

details.title: 48–72 hour recovery window
details.body: Muscles need 48–72 hours to repair micro-damage and grow. Proper weekly rhythm creates enough space between sessions targeting the same muscle group — this is the foundation of progressive overload.

details.title: 3 progressive adaptation phases
details.body: Phase 1 (weeks 1–2): 3 sessions/week — body learns load recognition. Phase 2 (weeks 3–6): 4 sessions — build strength base. Phase 3 (week 7+): 5–6 sessions — personalize by goal.

details.title: Choose sustainable rhythm, not ideal
details.body: 6 programs from 2 sessions/week (super busy) to 6/week (athlete). The best rhythm isn't the highest — it's the one you can maintain for 12 consecutive weeks.

tabs.title: Progress Ladder
tabs.longDesc: Progress that can't be measured isn't sustainable. The progress ladder shows you clearly where you are and what to do next. Combined with 3-period tests (Week 4, 8, 12) and a 4-dimension radar chart, you get a complete picture of physical health.

highlights.title: Clear ladder structure
highlights.desc: Know exactly the next step in your journey

highlights.title: Periodic 3-test cycles
highlights.desc: Tests at week 4, week 8, and week 12

tabs.quote: What can't be measured can't be improved. Small, measurable, consistent progress — that's the real formula.

details.title: Fair testing — not impulsive
details.body: 3 test periods (Weeks 4, 8, 12) are planned when fully recovered — not after a hard session. Consistent test conditions give reliable results.

details.title: 4-dimension radar — see hidden weaknesses
details.body: Strength · Endurance · Flexibility · Recovery. Many are strong but lack flexibility — a hidden injury risk that a single metric can't reveal.

details.title: 5 levels — know your position and destination
details.body: Level 1 (Basic Activity) to Level 5 (Athlete). Each level has clear criteria: exercises, reps/sets, recovery time. No more guessing 'how far have I come?'.

principles_full.keyFact: 6 fundamental movement patterns (Squat, Hinge, Push, Pull, Carry, Core) cover 95% of all fitness exercises needed for a lifetime.
principles_full.detail: Poor technique doesn't just cause injury — it wastes every session. Learning correctly from the start helps the brain record the right motor pattern, and the body executes it more efficiently over time. The human body is designed to perform 6 fundamental movement patterns. Mastering these 6 is enough to train for life — no complex equipment or fancy exercises needed.
details: Poor technique creates 'bad motor patterns' — the brain memorizes incorrect movement and automates it. Correcting later is much harder than learning correctly from the start.
6 fundamental movement patterns: Squat (sitting down), Hip Hinge (hip fold), Push (pressing), Pull (rowing), Carry (carrying), Core (stabilizing). Every complex exercise is a variation of these 6.
Correct technique with light weight is more effective than poor technique with heavy weight. The principle of 'progressive overload' is only safe when form is solid.
Self-recording video or a mirror is the most effective free tool for checking technique. Every 2 weeks, record 1 fundamental exercise and self-assess.
No gym or equipment needed: just 2 square meters of space, a mat, and bodyweight are enough to learn all 6 movement patterns correctly.

principles_full.keyFact: 3 sessions/week for 12 weeks = 36 sessions. 7 sessions/week for 3 weeks = 21 sessions then quit. The math supports consistency.
principles_full.detail: The brain builds 'neural superhighways' through regular repetition — not through high intensity. Neuromuscular adaptation occurs with appropriate stimulus, adequate rest, and stable repetition cycles. Training too much too soon elevates cortisol long-term, disrupts sleep, depletes willpower — and ultimately leads to quitting. Build consistency first, increase intensity later.
details: The brain needs 21–66 days to automate a new behavior. During this phase, willpower is a finite resource — design habits to consume the least willpower possible.
The 'minimum effective dose' principle: the minimum training stimulus still creates adaptation. 20 minutes with good form beats 90 minutes with fatigued form.
Recovery is not wasted time — it's when the body actually adapts and gets stronger. Skipping recovery breaks the adaptation cycle.
Habit stacking: attach your workout to an existing habit (after morning coffee, before showering). Reduces the 'friction' of starting.
When you miss a day: apply the 'never miss twice' rule. Missing 1 day is an incident; missing 2 consecutive days starts a new habit (the habit of not training).

points.label: 21–66 days
points.note: Time for the brain to automate a habit

points.label: Adequate recovery
points.note: Body adapts during rest, not training

principles_full.keyFact: Just 4 simple metrics: reps increased, plank time, waist circumference, and energy levels. No complex equipment needed.
principles_full.detail: Fitness progress happens slowly and non-linearly — without clear feedback, the brain can't distinguish 'making progress' from 'standing still'. Measurement creates a clear feedback loop: you know what to adjust, and more importantly, you see that you're actually progressing even if slowly.
details: 4 types of metrics to track: (1) Strength — reps/weight increase; (2) Endurance — plank time, step count; (3) Body composition — waist/hip measurement; (4) Function — energy levels, sleep quality.
4-week test cycle: not arbitrary — 4 weeks is enough to see clear adaptation without losing direction.
Record results with whatever tool works for you: phone notes, spreadsheet, handwritten journal. What matters is RECORDING, not the tool.
Compare with yourself last week, not with others. 5% improvement every 4 weeks after 1 year = 80% improvement from baseline.
When results don't change after 4 weeks: not failure — it's a signal to adjust (add load, change exercises, improve sleep/nutrition).

points.label: Body composition
points.note: Waist, hips — more meaningful than scale weight

points.label: 4-week cycle
points.note: Review & adjust on a regular schedule

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: HD Video Per Exercise — Why Watching Correctly Matters More Than Reading
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: Learning movement technique via video activates the brain's mirror neurons — the body begins learning the movement pattern even before practice. Watching from the correct angles reduces technique learning time by 40%.
highlight_modals_full.detail: Training technique cannot be learned from text alone. HD video from multiple angles allows the brain to analyze 3D movement — something 2D images or text descriptions simply cannot convey.
details: Mirror neurons: When you watch someone else perform a movement, the same motor-control brain regions in your own brain activate — this is the mechanism for learning movement through observation.

Camera angle matters: The side (sagittal) view shows squat depth and back position. The front (frontal) view shows bilateral symmetry. The rear view shows spinal alignment. A video covering all 3 angles is best.

Movement cues: 'Sit between your feet' is more effective than 'bend knees 90°'. 'Push the floor down' is more effective than 'extend the knee'. Good cues activate the right muscles better than pure technical descriptions.
Viewing speed: Watching slow-motion at 0.5× speed helps you spot movement phases that the naked eye misses at full speed — especially important for deadlifts and overhead press.

Level comparison: Watching the same exercise at beginner, intermediate and advanced levels side by side helps the brain build a visual roadmap of progress — knowing where you are and what the destination looks like.
Watch first, then practice: Motor Learning research shows watching video 2–3 times before practicing improves first-session technique by 28% compared to those who only read descriptions.

points.label: Mirror neurons
points.note: Brain learns technique while watching, before practice

points.label: Slow-motion 0.5×
points.note: Spot movement phases missed at full speed

points.label: +28% technique
points.note: Watching video before training beats reading descriptions

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: 3 Levels Per Exercise — Progress That Never Stalls
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: Progressive Overload principle: the body only keeps developing when stimulus gradually increases over time. 3 levels per exercise create a clear progression path for at least 6–18 months.
highlight_modals_full.detail: Most people quit training not because they're lazy — but because they hit a plateau and don't know what the next step is. 3 clear levels per exercise solve this: there's always something to aim for.
details: Level 1 — Basic (Beginner): Full range of motion with support or low load. Goal is learning the correct movement pattern, not volume. Example: Goblet squat with a light dumbbell.
Level 2 — Intermediate: Same movement pattern but less support or increased load. Technique is stable, now focus on strength progression. Example: Barbell back squat.
Level 3 — Advanced: Added difficulty through unilateral (one leg/arm), special tempo, or extended range. Examples: Pistol squat, pause squat, tempo squat 4-0-1-0.
Level-up criteria: Not impulsive — based on specific criteria (10 reps × 3 sets with perfect technique at current level). Don't level up before meeting the criteria.
Time between levels: Beginners typically take 4–8 weeks per level. Intermediate takes 8–16 weeks. There's no 'too slow' — only 'right time' or 'not yet ready'.
When stuck at a level: Not from lack of effort — usually from insufficient volume (add 1–2 sets), insufficient protein, or poor sleep. Fix these 3 factors before worrying about technique.

points.label: 6–18 month roadmap
points.note: 3 levels = sufficient challenge for at least 1.5 years

points.label: Level-up criteria
points.note: 10 reps × 3 sets with perfect form = ready

points.label: 4–8 weeks per level
points.note: Normal for beginners — don't compare with others

points.label: Plateau = lack of volume
points.note: Add 1–2 sets before worrying about technique

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: Science-Based Warm-Up — 5–8 Minutes You Can't Skip
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: Proper warm-up raises muscle temperature by 1–2°C, improves neuromuscular transmission, and reduces joint viscosity. Result: peak strength increases 15–20%, injury risk decreases 20–30%.
highlight_modals_full.detail: Warm-up isn't a ritual — it has specific physiological functions. Cold muscles contract less effectively, neural transmission is slower, and joints lack lubrication. 5–8 minutes of proper warm-up completely transforms session quality.
details: Muscle temperature: Each 1°C temperature increase = 2–4% faster muscle contraction speed. 5 minutes of warm-up is enough to raise deep muscle temperature by 1–2°C — equivalent to a 4–8% increase in contraction speed and strength.

Synovial fluid: In the morning or after prolonged sitting, joint fluid is thick and scarce. Light movement during warm-up stimulates synovial fluid secretion, reducing friction and risk of cartilage damage.

Neural pre-activation: Warm-up activates motor neurons needed in the session. Starting with exercises similar to the training pattern (mobility squat before a squat session) is more effective than general jogging.

Dynamic > Static: Dynamic warm-up (leg swings, hip circles, arm circles) is better than static stretching before training. Static stretch before training can temporarily reduce peak strength by 5–10%.
Progressive intensity: Start light → gradually increase intensity. Don't start immediately with your heaviest exercises. Rule of thumb: 2–3 warm-up sets at 50–70% of working weight before main sets.
Psychological warm-up: Warm-up time is also when the brain 'switches mode' from work/daily life to the training session. Don't skip this psychological warm-up — it affects focus and motivation.

points.label: Neural pre-activation
points.note: Activates the correct motor neurons you'll use

points.label: No static stretch before
points.note: Reduces peak strength by 5–10% if done before training

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: 4 Standard Time Blocks — Scientific Structure for Every Session
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: 4 blocks serve 4 different physiological functions: Warm-Up (neural activation) → Main Workout (stimulus) → Cool-Down (recovery initiation) → Mind Reset (ANS regulation). Missing any block reduces overall effectiveness.
highlight_modals_full.detail: The 4-block structure isn't arbitrary — each block serves a phase in the physiological cycle of a training session. When 1 block is missing, the entire physiological chain is broken and overall effectiveness decreases even if the main workout volume stays the same.
details: Block 1 — Warm-Up (5–10 min): Raises muscle temperature, activates neuromuscular systems, lubricates joints. Skipping = 15–20% reduction in peak strength and increased risk of sudden tendon strain.
Block 2 — Main Workout (10–150 min): The core of the session. Strength, cardio, or combined. This is the only block that can flex in duration — the others should stay consistent.

Block 3 — Cool-Down (5–10 min): Static stretch post-workout (not before) while muscles are warm helps increase range of motion and reduce DOMS. Hold each position ≥30 seconds — under 15 seconds has no effect.
Block 4 — Mind Reset (5 min): Adjusts the autonomic nervous system from sympathetic (fight/flight) to parasympathetic (rest/digest). Controlled breathing is the fastest way to achieve this.
Time ratios: For a 60-min session: Warm-Up 8' + Main 40' + Cool-Down 7' + Mind Reset 5'. For 20 min: 4' + 10' + 4' + 2'. The ratio flexes, the structure stays the same.

Common mistakes: Skipping warm-up because 'too busy', skipping cool-down because 'boring', skipping mind reset because 'not necessary'. The result is a session with only Block 2 — missing the 3 most important parts for sustainability.

points.label: Warm-up non-negotiable
points.note: +15–20% peak strength when warmed up properly

points.label: Main Workout
points.note: The only block fully flexible in duration

points.label: Cool-down after (not before)
points.note: ≥30 sec per position for real effect

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: 8 Time Levels — From 20 Minutes to 3 Hours, All Planned
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: 'Too busy to train today' is usually not about time — it's about lacking a plan for short sessions. 20 structured minutes is more effective than 1 unplanned hour.
highlight_modals_full.detail: 8 time levels from 20 to 180 minutes ensure there's always a suitable plan for however much time you have that day — no excuse to skip just because 'not enough time'.
details: Level 20 min (Super busy): Warm-Up 4' + Full-body circuit 12' + Quick stretch 3' + Breath 1'. 3 compound exercises (squat/push/hinge), 3 sets × 8 reps. Zero wasted seconds.
Level 30 min (Quick): Add 1 exercise or 1 set per exercise. Or replace circuits with supersets (2 exercises back-to-back, shorter rest).
Level 45 min (Standard): Can split into strength (25') + light cardio (10') or focus entirely on strength with more thorough warm-up.
Level 60 min (Complete): Enough time for focused lower or upper body training with full warm-up and meaningful cool-down. This is the 'ideal session' for most working adults.
Level 90–120 min (Advanced): Add accessory work after main lift, or combine strength + LISS cardio (low-intensity steady-state). Needs additional nutrition during/after the session.
Level 180 min (Intensive): Suitable for athletes or special training days. Requires special attention to hydration, intra-workout nutrition (carbs during session), and recovery afterward.

points.label: 20 minutes is enough
points.note: Structured full-body circuit is no worse than 1 hour

points.label: 8 levels = 8 ready plans
points.note: Always have a plan regardless of available time

points.label: 60 min = ideal
points.note: Enough for a complete session without time pressure

points.label: No 'too busy'
points.note: Only 'no plan for a short session yet'

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: Minute-by-Minute Detail — No More 'What to Train Next'
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: People who train with a specific minute-by-minute plan complete 94% of intended volume. Those without a detailed plan only complete 67% — skipping exercises, cutting sets short, resting too long.
highlight_modals_full.detail: Minute-by-minute planning doesn't mean being rigid — it means knowing exactly what you'll do in each phase. This clarity eliminates all 'dead time' (wasted time due to hesitation) from your session.
details: Dead time in sessions: Hesitation between exercises, deciding next sets, finding equipment. Gym surveys show dead time takes up 20–35% of time for unplanned gym sessions.
Rest timer vs. feel: Resting by feel tends to run 40% longer than necessary. Timer: 60–90 seconds for hypertrophy, 3–5 minutes for max strength effort. Being specific = more efficient.
Prioritize exercises: Train the most important exercise first when energy is highest. Accessory work last. If the session gets cut short, you've already completed the most important part.

Supersets and giant sets: Pair 2–3 exercises not targeting the same primary muscle group consecutively (e.g., squat + pull-up + plank). Increases density (volume/time) without extending total session time.
Simple tracking: Note immediately after each set (exercise, reps, weight). 2–3 minutes per session. Helps decide the next set quickly and build progression logic for the next session.
Adaptive planning: A minute-by-minute plan isn't unchangeable — it's a starting point. Adjust when needed (more tired than expected, missing equipment) but don't break the overall structure.

points.label: Prioritize first
points.note: Most important exercise first while energy is high

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: 3 Weekly Rhythm Phases — From Start to Personalization
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS, Selye 1950): the body responds to stress in 3 phases — Alarm (shock) → Resistance (adaptation) → Exhaustion (if not rested). A 3-phase weekly rhythm reflects this physiological cycle.
highlight_modals_full.detail: 3 weekly rhythm phases aren't arbitrarily set — they reflect how the body learns to adapt to training load over time. Skipping any phase leads to injury or failure to achieve results.
details: Phase 1 — Start (Weeks 1–4): 3 sessions/week, low-moderate intensity, focused on learning technique. Goal: build the habit, not fitness. No need to train to muscular failure.
Phase 2 — Build (Weeks 5–12): 4 sessions/week, controlled volume and intensity increase. This is the main muscle gain/fat loss phase — the body is adapting fastest.
Phase 3 — Advance (Week 13+): 5–6 sessions/week, personalized for specific goals. Only enter this phase when the base is solid enough — no shortcuts.
Deload weeks: After every 4–6 weeks of increasing volume, 1 week at 40–50% reduced intensity. Supercompensation occurs during this deload week — it's actually the strongest week physiologically.

Why you can't skip the 3 phases: Starting directly in Phase 3 (5–6 sessions/week) = overuse injury within 4–8 weeks. ACSM statistics: 70% of people who train too much too soon get injured within the first 3 months.
Phase transitions: No specific day to 'enter a new phase' — based on body signals: good recovery (no lingering pain), stable performance, good sleep, stable mood.

points.label: Phase 1: Build habits
points.note: Learn technique + build habit — not fitness yet

points.label: Phase 3: Personalize
points.note: Week 13+: optimize for your specific goal

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: 6 Goal-Based Programs — Find the Rhythm That Suits You Best
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: 'One size fits all' doesn't exist in training. 6 programs designed for 6 different profiles in terms of goal, available time, and starting point. Choosing the wrong program = no results despite hard effort.
highlight_modals_full.detail: Many people fail not from lack of discipline — but because they're following a program that doesn't fit their situation. A beginner following a professional athlete's schedule, or a busy person trying to maintain 6 sessions/week — neither is sustainable.
details: Program 1 — Super Busy (2 sessions/week): Full-body each session, 45 minutes, 4–5 compound exercises. Sufficient to maintain muscle and overall health. Suitable for: people working >50 hours/week or with major family responsibilities.

Program 2 — Beginner (3 sessions/week): A/B alternating (Full-body A and Full-body B alternating). Most effective for beginners because frequency is high enough to learn technique without overloading.
Program 3 — Popular (4 sessions/week): Upper/Lower split. 2 upper days, 2 lower days. Enough for notable progress with sufficient rest between sessions. Suitable for: most non-professional people.

Program 4 — Advanced (5 sessions/week): Push/Pull/Legs or Upper-Lower-Full. Requires solid technique foundation and high recovery capacity. Not suitable for people under high stress or with poor sleep.
Program 5 — Intensive (6 sessions/week): Train each muscle group separately (bro split) or Daily Undulating Periodization. Requires 12+ months experience and optimal nutrition-sleep conditions.

Program 6 — Athlete (6 sessions + supplementary cardio): Combines strength training, sport-specific cardio, and mobility work. Not a goal everyone needs to reach — but shows the potential for development.

points.label: Programs 1–2: Start
points.note: 2–3 sessions/week for beginners and busy people

points.label: Choose based on reality
points.note: Sustainable rhythm > ideal rhythm you can't maintain

points.label: Build gradually
points.note: Stable for 4 weeks then add 1 session — no skipping

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: Proper Rest — Recovery Is Essential, Not Laziness
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: Muscles don't grow stronger during training — but during rest afterward. A rest day isn't a day of 'doing nothing' — it's when the body actually builds what you stimulated during the session.
highlight_modals_full.detail: The 'no pain no gain' and 'rest is for the weak' culture has harmed millions of athletes. Adequate rest isn't a sign of weakness — it's an essential training skill used by professional athletes.
details: Active recovery vs. passive rest: Rest days don't mean lying still. 20–30 minutes of walking, light yoga, or light swimming at low intensity (<60% max HR) actually speeds up recovery by increasing blood flow without creating additional load.

Sleep is recovery tool #1: Growth hormone (GH) is secreted 70–80% during slow-wave sleep. Missing 1 hour of sleep = 18–21% reduction in muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and increased cortisol. No supplement compensates for poor sleep.

Nutrition on rest days: Don't reduce protein on rest days — muscle protein synthesis continues 24–48h post-workout. Carbs can be slightly reduced but don't eliminate — glycogen needs to be replenished.

HRV (Heart Rate Variability): Simplest metric to measure recovery. High morning HRV = good recovery. Low HRV over multiple consecutive days = need more rest or reduce intensity. Many smartwatches measure this.
Resting Heart Rate trend: If RHR increases 5–10 BPM above baseline for 3+ consecutive days — this is an overtraining signal. Need 1–2 extra rest days or 40–50% volume reduction.

Psychological recovery: Rest days are also psychological recovery. Training every day without enthusiasm, forcing yourself — this is a signal to rest even if the body 'doesn't hurt'. Motivation burnout typically comes before physical burnout.

points.label: Active recovery better
points.note: Light walk > lying still on rest days

points.label: Sleep = GH +70–80%
points.note: No supplement compensates for poor sleep

points.label: HRV tracks recovery
points.note: Smartwatch measures it — high HRV = recovered

points.label: Psychological burnout first
points.note: Lost motivation is an earlier signal than physical pain

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: Clear Progress Ladder — Know Exactly What Your Next Step Is
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: Lack of clarity about 'the next step' is the #1 reason people quit training (IHRSA 2019). Not laziness, not lack of time — but 'I don't know what I need to do next'.
highlight_modals_full.detail: The progress ladder isn't a title or competition. It's a positioning system — helping you know where you are now, what's needed to advance, and what the next step looks like specifically.
details: The problem with 'free training': No clear criteria = not knowing when you're 'good enough'. Training without knowing if you're progressing = losing motivation after 4–8 weeks.
5 clear levels with specific criteria: Level 1 (walk 30'/day) → Level 2 (10 push-ups, plank 30") → Level 3 (bodyweight squat, run 2km) → Level 4 (squat 1.5BW, 5km <30') → Level 5 (athlete).
Why 5 levels, not more: Granular enough to know where you are, not so many that it causes overwhelm. 5 levels also aligns with about 1–5 years of serious training.
Testing into the right level: Assess yourself based on objective criteria (reps, time, load), not feelings. Many people overestimate or underestimate their actual level.

Rewards for leveling up: New exercise types (unilateral, olympic lifting), increased training frequency, or adding specialized cardio. Each level unlocks new capabilities — this is the dynamic reward.
Don't compare with others: The ladder is personal — based on your own baseline, not others' benchmarks. A 50-year-old at Level 3 is much better than a 20-year-old at Level 3 who is plateauing.

points.label: Clear positioning
points.note: Knowing where you are = 70% less likely to quit

points.label: Rewards for leveling up
points.note: Each level unlocks new capabilities and exercises

points.label: Don't compare
points.note: The ladder is personal — your own baseline

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: 3-Period Testing — Weeks 4, 8, and 12 Are Key Milestones
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: What gets measured gets managed (Peter Drucker). 3 test periods in the first 12 weeks allow adjustments based on real data — not feelings. People with a specific test schedule achieve goals 2.5× more effectively.
highlight_modals_full.detail: 3 test periods aren't about checking up — they're about adjusting. Week 4 shows whether the plan is working. Week 8 reveals the progression rate. Week 12 gives a full evaluation and sets the plan for the next phase.
details: Week 4 test — Calibration: After 4 weeks, the body has passed the initial neural adaptation phase. This test shows whether the plan is suitable (progressing) or needs adjustment (not progressing significantly).
Week 8 test — Trend analysis: Compare with week 4. If progress >10% = plan is working well. If <5% = review nutrition and sleep. If performance decreased = overtraining.
Week 12 test — Full evaluation: Comprehensive assessment of all 4 dimensions (strength, endurance, flexibility, recovery). These results form the foundation for designing the next 12-week plan.
Testing on the right day: Don't test after a heavy session, when tired or sick, or after a poor night's sleep. Consistent conditions allow accurate comparison between periods.
Adjustments based on tests: Week 4 test poor → increase protein or sleep before changing volume. Week 8 test good → increase volume by 5–10%. Don't change multiple things at once.
Create a ritual: Turn test day into a ceremony — same time, same warm-up, same music if applicable. Rituals help the mind enter the right state and produce more consistent results.

points.label: Week 4: Calibration
points.note: Is the plan working? Adjust early if needed

points.label: Week 8: Trend
points.note: >10% progress = heading in the right direction

points.label: Create a test ritual
points.note: Same conditions each time = reliable results

highlight_modals_full.modalTitle: 4-Dimension Radar Chart — Strength · Endurance · Flexibility · Recovery
highlight_modals_full.keyFact: The 4 dimensions aren't 4 separate tests — they're a comprehensive physical health assessment system. VO2 max (endurance) is the #1 predictor of longevity according to a JAMA 2018 study of 122,000 people.
highlight_modals_full.detail: Fitness isn't one-dimensional. The strongest person isn't necessarily the healthiest. The most enduring person isn't necessarily recovering well. A 4-dimension radar chart is the simplest way to see the 'complete picture' of physical health — not just strengths.
details: Dimension 1 — Strength: Measures ability to produce force. Simple tests: max push-up reps, 5RM squat, 3RM deadlift. Strength is the foundation — lacking strength limits all other dimensions.

Dimension 2 — Endurance (Cardiovascular): VO2 max is the gold standard but hard to measure. Alternatives: 1.5km run time, beep test, or 12-minute Cooper test. VO2 max is the strongest predictor of cardiovascular mortality and longevity.

Dimension 3 — Flexibility (Mobility): Not about being as flexible as a dancer — but having enough range of motion to safely perform fundamental movement patterns. Tests: overhead squat, hip flexor length, shoulder mobility.

Dimension 4 — Recovery: Composite of HRV trend, resting heart rate, sleep quality (PSQI score), and time to recover from DOMS after a standard session. This dimension improves when the other 3 are balanced.
Asymmetry is a warning sign: If one dimension is >30% lower than others → prioritize improving that dimension in the next phase. Don't try to optimize strengths when there's a clear weakness.

How to draw the radar chart: Score each dimension 1–10 based on the progress ladder criteria (Level 1 = 2 points, Level 2 = 4 points, etc.). Draw on 4 axes and connect into a quadrilateral. Goal: the most even shape, not the highest score on one axis.

points.label: Score 1–10 per dimension
points.note: Based on progress ladder criteria — objective

points.label: Even quadrilateral
points.note: Goal: balance — not high score in just one dimension

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: Why Only 6 Patterns? — The Biomechanics Behind Thousands of Exercises
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Biomechanists analyzed >3,000 exercises and found all of them are variations of 6 fundamental movement patterns. Master the 6 = foundation for 95% of all exercises in your lifetime.
detail_modals_full.detail: The 6-pattern framework wasn't arbitrarily invented — it's the result of biomechanical analysis from thousands of different exercises. Each pattern represents a joint-muscle chain coordinating in a way the human body was evolutionarily designed for.
details: Squat (kneeling): Simultaneous hip + knee + ankle flexion — activates 60–70% of total body muscle mass, most important for lower-body strength.
Hip Hinge: Hip flexion while keeping spine neutral — foundation of deadlift, Romanian DL, kettlebell swing. Glutes and hamstrings develop maximally.
Push: From floor push-up to overhead press — develops chest, shoulder, tricep along horizontal and vertical axes.
Pull: From band pull to pull-up — balances the push pattern, develops back, biceps, rhomboids. Reduces risk of rounded shoulders from excessive pushing.
Carry: Walking with load — activates core 360°, improves posture, mimics functional movement in real life.
Core & Breath (anti-movement/collapse): Plank, dead bug, pallof press — not sit-ups, but resisting unwanted movement. Breathing is the baseline condition for all other patterns.

points.label: Full-body coverage
points.note: 6 patterns = 100% major muscle groups activated evenly

points.label: Unlimited variations
points.note: Each pattern has 5–15+ variations from easy to very hard

points.label: Long-term safety
points.note: No structural weak points are left unaddressed

points.label: Easy to remember
points.note: Design your own session with just 1 exercise per pattern

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: Unlimited Variations — Same Pattern, Endless Levels of Progress
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Each pattern has a spectrum from extremely easy to extremely difficult within the same progression chain. No need to switch exercises — just move up the spectrum when ready.
detail_modals_full.detail: The most common mistake in training is constantly changing exercises instead of going deeper into one pattern. Chair squat → goblet squat → barbell squat → pistol squat: same pattern, four different levels.
details: Regression: Every pattern has a super-easy version for beginners, injury recovery, or fatigued days. There's never 'no exercise to do'.
Progression: Add load, reduce support, increase range, change tempo — 4 axes of progress for each pattern without needing additional equipment.
Unilateral (one leg/arm): Pistol squat, single-leg RDL, archer push-up — doubles difficulty without heavier weights. Reveals bilateral imbalances.
Tempo: 4-second eccentric instead of 1 second increases time under tension (TUT) by 300–400%. Same weight, much harder, more effective for muscle growth.
Environment: Sand, uneven floor, sandbags instead of barbells — change the stability factor without changing the fundamental pattern.
Transfer ability: Master the goblet squat → barbell squat becomes easier immediately; master push-ups → bench press is instant. Same pattern, different tool.

points.label: Clear progress
points.note: Know exactly what the next step requires

points.label: No equipment needed
points.note: Bodyweight is enough to reach intermediate-advanced level

points.label: Long-term consistency
points.note: Never boring with a clear progression spectrum

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: Full-Body Balance — Designed With No Weak Points
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Most sports injuries aren't from weakness — but from imbalance. Too much Push without enough Pull → shoulder pain. Too much Squat without enough Hinge → lower back pain.
detail_modals_full.detail: The human body evolved to perform these 6 movements in a balanced ratio. When training too much of one pattern and neglecting the opposing pattern, muscular imbalances appear and injury is only a matter of time.
details: Push + Pull: A 1:1 volume ratio between pushing and pulling reduces shoulder pain risk by 60%. Many gym-goers push 3× more than they pull — this is the most common cause of rotator cuff injuries.
Squat + Hinge: Squats develop the quads (front of thighs), Hinges develop glutes/hamstrings (back of thighs). Standard quad:hamstring ratio is 3:2; imbalance → knee injury.
Bilateral + Unilateral: Barbell squats are great for strength, but single-leg squats reveal bilateral imbalances. Add at least 1 unilateral exercise per pattern per week.
Core anti-movement: The spine isn't designed to bend under load — but to resist unwanted movement. Plank is better than crunches for back health.
Breath under load: Valsalva maneuver when lifting heavy protects the spine. Poor breathing = unstable core = harmful load on spinal discs.
Suggested weekly training ratio: 2× squat + 2× hinge + 2× push + 2× pull + 2× carry + daily core/breath = no structural weak points.

points.label: Injury prevention
points.note: Balanced push/pull reduces shoulder pain risk 60%

points.label: Breath is the foundation
points.note: Proper breathing protects the spine under any load

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: The Brain Needs Structure — Make Fewer Decisions, Train Better
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Baumeister (1998) research on 'decision fatigue' shows each small decision depletes willpower. People with a structured training plan maintain consistency 62% vs 23% in those without a plan (Annesi, 2003).
detail_modals_full.detail: Entering the gym without knowing what to do forces the brain to constantly make decisions: what to train, how many sets, how long to rest. That energy would be better spent on training quality. Structure eliminates this problem entirely.
details: Decision fatigue in training: Every time you decide 'what to do next' mid-session, decision quality decreases. Result: trailing off toward the end of the session, skipping hard exercises, cutting time short.
Structured plan → automatic execution: When you know exactly what you'll do, the brain shifts to 'auto-pilot'. Technical quality and intensity both improve because the brain isn't busy planning.
Lower barrier to start: 'I'll do A → B → C' is easier to start than 'what should I train today?' Low startup barrier = fewer missed sessions.
Habit stacking: Structure allows attaching training to existing habits. 'After dinner → 5-minute warm-up' is more sustainable than 'I'll train sometime tonight'.
Flexibility within structure: Have 45 minutes instead of 60? Proportionally reduce each block's time. The framework stays the same — the content flexes.
Long-term adherence: A 12-month study (Conn et al., 2011) found the structured group maintained 68% of sessions vs 34% in the unstructured group.

points.label: 62% vs 23%
points.note: Consistency rate with/without a structured plan

points.label: Easier to start
points.note: Low barrier when you already know exactly what to do

points.label: Smart flexibility
points.note: Structure flexes with available time, doesn't break

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: 4 Time Blocks — A Universal Structure from 20 to 180 Minutes
detail_modals_full.keyFact: 4 blocks (Warm-Up → Main Workout → Cool-Down → Mind Reset) serve 4 different physiological functions that can't replace each other. Removing any block reduces effectiveness and increases risk.
detail_modals_full.detail: Each block isn't arbitrary — they serve a specific physiological function. Warm-Up activates the neuromuscular system. Main Workout creates the growth stimulus. Cool-Down supports recovery. Mind Reset regulates the autonomic nervous system.
details: Warm-Up (5–10 min): Raises muscle temperature by 1–2°C, increases joint fluid viscosity, activates neuromuscular transmission. Skipping = 15–20% reduction in peak strength and increased tendon injury risk.
Main Workout (10–150 min): The core — strength, cardio, or combined. This is the only block that can be fully extended or shortened based on available time.
Cool-Down (5–10 min): Static stretch post-workout reduces DOMS by 20–40%. Minimum hold time 30 seconds/position for real effect — less than that doesn't count.
Mind Reset (5 min): Cyclic sighing activates the parasympathetic system, reduces cortisol, prepares the brain for the rest of the day. Not optional — it's the best recovery investment.
When shortening a session: Prioritize keeping warm-up + mind reset intact. Cut from main workout. A 20-min session: 5' + 10' + 3' + 2' — still all 4 blocks.

Flexible order within main workout block: Strength before cardio if muscle gain is the goal. Cardio before strength if cardiovascular endurance is the goal. 4 blocks stay the same, content within blocks is flexible.

points.label: Main Workout
points.note: The only block fully flexible in duration

points.label: Mind Reset is investment
points.note: 5 minutes = better recovery for 23 remaining hours

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: 5-Minute Mind Reset — Cortisol, Recovery, and Better Sleep
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Stanford research (Spiegel et al., 2023) shows cyclic sighing reduces cortisol by 15% and improves positive affect more than mindfulness meditation or box breathing in 5 minutes of practice.
detail_modals_full.detail: 5 minutes post-workout is when cortisol is at its peak. If you rush out immediately, this elevated cortisol follows you through the rest of your day, affecting nighttime sleep and muscle recovery.
details: Post-workout cortisol: Exercise is good stress (eustress), but cortisol rises during and after training. Without proper reduction → difficult nighttime sleep, slower muscle recovery.

Cyclic sighing: Inhale fully through nose → take another short sniff through nose → exhale long and slow through mouth. Repeat 5–10 times. Activates the parasympathetic system faster than any other breathing technique.
Box breathing (4-4-4-4): Good alternative if not comfortable with cyclic sighing. Inhale 4 sec → hold 4 → exhale 4 → hold 4. Used by special forces to reduce cortisol before/after missions.
Don't lie down: Sit or stand, eyes closed or focused on a fixed point. Lying down may lead to falling asleep, disrupting nighttime sleep schedule.
Improved sleep: People who train in the evening + 5-minute mind reset sleep 18% more deeply than those who stop training abruptly. Melatonin isn't suppressed by cortisol.
Cumulative benefits: Groups that consistently practice 5 minutes of mind reset post-workout for 8 weeks have 12% lower baseline cortisol levels and significantly lower self-reported stress.

points.label: Cortisol -15%
points.note: Cyclic sighing most effective in 5 minutes

points.label: Sleep 18% deeper
points.note: Especially when training in the evening

points.label: Better muscle recovery
points.note: Lower cortisol = higher GH during deep sleep

points.label: Calm is not weakness
points.note: Mind reset is a skill, not a sign of weakness

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: The 48–72 Hour Recovery Window — Muscles Grow at Rest, Not During Training
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Muscle Protein Synthesis (MPS) peaks 24–36 hours after training and returns to baseline after 48–72 hours. Training the same muscle group within 24 hours = disrupts regeneration. Training after 72 hours = missing the growth window.
detail_modals_full.detail: The paradox of training is that muscles don't get stronger during the workout — but during rest afterward. Training creates micro-damage in muscle fibers. The body repairs these micro-tears bigger and stronger — but only when given sufficient time.
details: Muscle Protein Synthesis (MPS): After strength training, MPS increases 25–150% and sustains for 24–48 hours. This is the most critical window for protein from meals to be used for muscle regeneration.

DOMS (Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness): Soreness 24–72 hours after training is a sign of micro-damage being repaired — not dangerous, but training heavily on the same muscle group during DOMS slows regeneration.

Glycogen resynthesis: After high-intensity cardio, muscle glycogen needs 24–48 hours to fully replenish with a normal diet. Training again when glycogen is low = poor performance and more muscle used as fuel.

CNS fatigue: The central nervous system becomes fatigued after heavy sessions. Can't be measured by muscle sensation alone — even when legs don't hurt, the CNS may not have recovered from heavy squats.
Growth hormone during sleep: GH is most secreted during slow-wave sleep, suppressed by high cortisol. Adequate rest and sleep are essential conditions for MPS to occur maximally.

Weekly rhythm design principles: Same primary muscle group at least 48 hours apart (ideally 72 hours). Upper/lower split alternating rather than consecutive. Active recovery on rest days doesn't impair recovery if intensity is low.

points.label: MPS peaks 24–48h
points.note: When protein from meals is used most

points.label: Rest 48–72h
points.note: Same muscle group — not sooner, not later

points.label: GH during deep sleep
points.note: Growth hormone mainly secreted in slow-wave sleep

points.label: CNS fatigues too
points.note: Central nervous system recovers slower than muscles

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: 3 Adaptation Phases — Sustainable Progress Without Burnout
detail_modals_full.keyFact: SAID Principle (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand): the body only adapts to the specific type of stimulus imposed. 3 adaptation phases (neural → structural → performance) occur sequentially and cannot be skipped.
detail_modals_full.detail: One of the most common mistakes beginners make is increasing too fast — more training days, more volume, more intensity — before the body has completed the first adaptation phase. The result is usually injury or burnout.
details: Phase 1 — Neural (Weeks 1–4): Not muscles growing but the brain learning to recruit more motor units. Strength increases 20–40% in the first 4 weeks = neural optimization, not hypertrophy.
Phase 2 — Structural (Weeks 5–12): True hypertrophy begins — protein is added to muscle fibers. Requires adequate protein (1.6–2.2g/kg/day) and sufficient sleep (7–9 hours) for this phase to occur.
Phase 3 — Performance (Week 13+): Body has the foundation → can optimize for specific goals (maximum strength, endurance, speed). True personalization begins here.
Structured deload: After 4–6 weeks of consecutive volume increases, 1 week at 40–50% reduced load allows supercompensation (above-baseline recovery). No deload = gradual performance decline.
Overtraining signs: Performance decreases despite adequate rest, resting heart rate 5–10 BPM above baseline for 3+ days, persistently poor mood, poor sleep without other cause.

Linear vs non-linear progression: Beginners → linear (same load increase each week). Intermediate and above → non-linear (heavy/medium/light week alternating). Failing to recognize this transition = early plateau.

points.label: Weeks 1–4: Neural
points.note: Brain learns, muscles don't grow yet — strength +20–40%

points.label: Weeks 5–12: Hypertrophy
points.note: Muscles mature with adequate protein + sleep

points.label: Week 13+: Personalized
points.note: Foundation built → optimize for your specific goal

points.label: Deload is mandatory
points.note: 1 week reduced load after 4–6 weeks to supercompensate

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: Sustainable Training Rhythm — The Best Rhythm Is the One You Can Maintain for 12 Months
detail_modals_full.keyFact: '2 sessions/week × 12 months = 96 sessions' beats '6 sessions/week × 6 weeks = 36 sessions'. Total accumulated volume long-term, not short-term intensity, determines real results.
detail_modals_full.detail: Fitness culture often glorifies high intensity and frequent training. But the most consistent long-term research shows the most important variable isn't intensity — it's consistency. Someone training 2 sessions/week for 5 years achieves better results than someone training 5/week for 6 months then quitting.
details: Minimum Effective Dose (MED): 2 strength sessions/week is enough to maintain and build muscle for non-professionals. No need to train more if you can't sustain it — start with the MED.

Never miss twice rule: Missing 1 session = normal. Missing 2 consecutive sessions = starting to lose momentum. The simplest rule to maintain consistency is never allowing 2 consecutive missed sessions.
6 programs from few to many: Super busy (2/week) → Beginner (3) → Popular (4) → Advanced (5) → Intensive (6) → Athlete (6 + supplementary cardio).
Scale up gradually: Maintain consistency at a lower level for 4 weeks then add 1 session. Don't jump from 2 to 5 — burnout arrives very quickly.
Social accountability: Training with 1 other person increases adherence by 37% (Plante et al., 1996). No partner? Online community or check-in apps also work.
Identity shift: People who maintain 12+ months typically no longer 'try to train' — they've become 'a person who trains'. Identity-based habits are more durable than goal-based habits.

points.label: Identity shift
points.note: 'I am a person who trains' is more durable than 'trying'

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: Periodic Testing — Measure Accurately for Reliable Progress
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Performing tests is a separate skill that takes 2–3 sessions to master. Inconsistent test conditions (after heavy training, poor sleep) can change results by ±15–20%, making you think you've progressed or regressed incorrectly.
detail_modals_full.detail: Fitness testing isn't just 'training and counting'. For results to be meaningful and comparable over time, test conditions must be consistent: same time of day, same sleep state, same warm-up, same equipment.
details: Schedule tests in advance: 3 test periods — Week 4, Week 8, Week 12 — placed in the calendar from the start, not dependent on feeling 'ready'. Test day is not a heavy training day.
Standardized test conditions: 8+ hours sleep the night before, no heavy training 48 hours prior, same time slot (e.g., Saturday morning), same 10-minute warm-up. Record all conditions.
±15–20% variation is not real progress: If test conditions differ, different results don't reflect actual fitness. Only compare tests with the same conditions.

Testing is a skill requiring practice: The first test is often suboptimal because of performance pressure unfamiliarity. Week 4 test = learning how to test. Week 8 and 12 = reliable data for comparison.
Detailed record-keeping: Record not just results but also subjective feeling (1–10), previous night's sleep, caffeine intake, weather. This metadata explains outliers.
Choose tests matching your goal: Muscle gain → 5RM squat/deadlift. Endurance → 2km run or beep test. Flexibility → sit-and-reach. Recovery → resting heart rate trend.

points.label: Consistent conditions
points.note: Same time, sleep, warm-up each test

points.label: Testing is a skill
points.note: First 1–2 sessions to learn, 3+ for reliable data

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: 4-Dimension Radar Chart — See Hidden Weaknesses a Single Metric Can't Show
detail_modals_full.keyFact: Someone with high strength but poor flexibility has a higher injury risk than a well-rounded trainer, even if they're 'stronger' in the conventional sense. 4 dimensions reveal hidden imbalances invisible through 1 metric.
detail_modals_full.detail: Fitness isn't one-dimensional. The strong person may lack endurance. The enduring person may lack strength. The flexible person may recover slowly. A 4-dimension radar chart shows the 'real picture' of your physical condition — not just your strengths.
details: Dimension 1 — Strength: Measured by representative test (squat BW ×1.5 for men, ×1.0 for women is a decent level). Strength is the foundation — lacking strength limits all other dimensions.
Dimension 2 — Endurance: VO2 max or simpler test like 1.5km run. VO2 max is the strongest predictor of cardiovascular mortality — more important than most other health metrics.
Dimension 3 — Flexibility: Not just for dancers — having enough range of motion to safely perform basic movement patterns. Lacking flexibility = compensation patterns = injury.
Dimension 4 — Recovery: Composite of HRV trend (decreasing = good), resting heart rate, sleep quality (PSQI <5), and subjective recovery time after a standard heavy session.
Asymmetry is a warning sign: Strong + inflexible = rotator cuff injury, hip impingement. Enduring + no strength base = stress fracture. Strong + poor recovery = cumulative overtraining.
How to use the radar chart: Draw at weeks 1, 4, 8, 12. The most concave dimension = prioritize training for the next phase. Goal: not the highest score on each dimension — but the most even shape.

points.label: Strong + stiff = dangerous
points.note: Hidden imbalance is a common injury cause

points.label: More even shape
points.note: Goal: balance — not the highest score on 1 dimension

detail_modals_full.modalTitle: 5 Progress Levels — Know Your Exact Position and What Comes Next
detail_modals_full.keyFact: 20–30% of people who quit training within 90 days don't do so from laziness — but because they don't know where they are or what the next step is (IHRSA, 2019). The level structure directly addresses this.
detail_modals_full.detail: 5 levels aren't a title or competition — they're a map. Knowing you're at Level 2 and what the criteria to reach Level 3 are = clear direction = less likely to quit. No map = getting lost.
details: Level 1 — Basic Activity: Walk 30 minutes/day, 3 times/week. No gym needed. This is the starting point for completely sedentary people. Goal: build the habit of movement before thinking about intensity.
Level 2 — Foundation: Can complete 3 sessions/week with 6 fundamental patterns at basic level (10 push-ups, goblet squat BW × 20 reps, plank 30 seconds). Most beginners achieve this in 4–8 weeks.
Level 3 — Intermediate: Sufficient strength to squat BW, deadlift BW ×1.2, 20 push-ups. Endurance: run 2km without stopping. This is the 'basically healthy' level by medical standards.
Level 4 — Advanced: Squat BW ×1.5 (men) / ×1.0 (women). 5km <30 minutes. Pull-up 5 reps (men) / 2 reps (women). Requires 6–18 months of systematic training from zero.
Level 5 — Athlete: Squat BW ×2.0+. 5km <22 minutes. Requires good genetics + long time + specialized programming. Not a goal everyone needs to reach.
Reality: 80% of health benefits come from Levels 1–3. No need for Levels 4–5 to have good health and longevity. Knowing this reduces pressure and helps maintain long-term consistency.

points.label: Level = map
points.note: Knowing position + next step = less likely to quit

points.label: Levels 1–3 = sufficient
points.note: 80% of health benefits from foundation to intermediate

b0.desc_body: (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the total calories your body burns daily — composed of 3 parts:

benefits.title: Eat on Target

b0.accuracy_body: Mifflin-St Jeor formula has a ±10–15% error margin because it cannot account for muscle-to-fat ratio. Use TDEE as a starting point — track your weight for 1–2 weeks. If stable, what you're currently eating IS your real TDEE.

mantras.desc: The body needs enough energy to function, recover and build muscle. Extreme calorie cuts slow metabolism and cause unwanted muscle loss.
mantras.keyFact: 2018 study (JAMA): eating adequate calories with the right composition outperforms strict calorie restriction by 40%
mantras.detail: Many people assume cutting calories as much as possible is best. But the body adapts: prolonged energy deficits reduce metabolic rate by 10–20%, thyroid hormones drop, and the body begins breaking down muscle for fuel. A deficit of 300–500 kcal/day is the safe zone for fat loss without muscle loss.
tips: 1,600–2,400 kcal/day depending on activity level
Don't consistently skip breakfast
Eat slowly — the brain needs 20 minutes to sense fullness

mantras.desc: Your biological clock works best when fed on schedule. Regular meal timing stabilizes blood sugar and controls unusual cravings.
mantras.keyFact: People who eat breakfast consistently have a BMI 1.5 points lower on average than those who regularly skip it
mantras.detail: Cortisol — the alertness hormone — peaks in the morning and declines through a 24h cycle. When you eat on schedule, the digestive biological clock syncs with this cycle: digestive enzymes secrete at their strongest and nutrient absorption is optimized. Skipping meals creates abnormal insulin spikes at the next meal, leading to more efficient fat storage.
tips: 3 main meals within the same time frame each day
Don't go more than 5 consecutive hours without eating
Prepare food in advance so you never skip meals

mantras.desc: Whole foods retain their micronutrients, fiber and natural enzymes. Ultra-processed foods trigger overeating through neurological mechanisms.
mantras.keyFact: Ultra-processed food accounts for 60% of average daily calories for urban dwellers today
mantras.detail: Ultra-processed food (UPF) is engineered to bypass natural fullness mechanisms: combining salt + sugar + fat at ratios that maximize dopamine activation. NIH 2019 research found people on a UPF diet consume an extra 500 kcal/day compared to those eating whole foods, even with the same food volume. Micronutrients (vitamin B complex, zinc, iron) in whole foods are critical for metabolism.
tips: Prioritize vegetables, fresh meat, eggs, fish
Read ingredient labels before buying
Rule of thumb: fewer than 5 ingredients per product

mantras.desc: Keto, IF, low-carb can all work — but only when suited to your body, lifestyle and specific goals. No single diet fits everyone.
mantras.keyFact: After 2 years, the success rate of every diet is equivalent if there's adequate protein and lifestyle compatibility
mantras.detail: A 2020 meta-analysis (NEJM) comparing 14 popular diets: after 6 months, the difference in weight loss between diets was only 1–2kg. The deciding factors aren't the diet's name but: (1) sustainable calorie deficit, (2) adequate protein, (3) lifestyle compatibility. Keto suits sedentary people; High-carb suits athletes; IF suits busy people.
tips: Define your goals clearly first
Test consistently for at least 4 weeks
Measure results objectively with data

mantras.sub: Veggies are allies, carbs are fuel
mantras.desc: Protein (1.6–2.2g/kg body weight) protects muscle, increases satiety and burns extra calories through digestion. The most important macro for any goal.
mantras.keyFact: Increasing protein from 15% to 30% of total calories naturally reduces intake by 441 kcal/day without counting calories
mantras.detail: Protein has the highest Thermic Effect of the 3 macros: digesting protein burns 20–30% of its own calorie content, vs. carbs at 5–10% and fat at 0–3%. This means 100 kcal of protein only provides 70–80 kcal net. Leucine in animal protein activates mTOR — the primary signaling pathway for muscle synthesis. Distributing 30–40g protein evenly across 3–4 meals is more optimal than concentrating it in 1–2 meals.
tips: 1.6–2.2g protein/kg body weight/day
Include a protein source in every meal
Eggs, meat, legumes, Greek yogurt

mantras.desc: One pizza meal doesn't make you fat, just as one salad doesn't make you lean. Results come from weekly habits, not a single meal.
mantras.keyFact: 'The 90/10 rule': maintaining 90% good habits allows 10% flexibility while still achieving long-term results
mantras.detail: A 'cheat meal' of about 1,000–1,500 kcal can affect weight by 0.2–0.4kg — mostly glycogen and retained water, not actual fat. The added glycogen will deplete within 1–2 subsequent days. The real danger is the 'already ruined, might as well continue' mindset (all-or-nothing thinking). Strategy: plan flexible meals rather than letting them happen on impulse.
tips: 1–2 flexible meals/week is normal
Return to your regular routine immediately after
Don't 'compensate' by skipping meals

mantras.sub: Best diet is the one you can keep
mantras.desc: A perfect diet in theory that can't be maintained in practice is worthless. 80% consistent for 1 year always beats 100% perfect for 3 weeks then quitting.
mantras.keyFact: Eating habits take an average of 66 days to form (not 21 days as commonly believed)
mantras.detail: 'Identity-based habits' (James Clear): instead of saying 'I want to eat healthy', say 'I am someone who prioritizes health'. Every time you choose to eat right, you're voting for that identity. Sustainability comes from reducing friction: preparing food in advance, placing vegetables at eye level in the fridge. Willpower is a limited resource — systems are unlimited.
tips: Start with the smallest possible change
Build systems — don't rely on willpower
Modify favorite dishes instead of eliminating them

fat-loss.headline: Sustainable fat loss — preserve every pound of muscle
fat-loss.science: A 300–500 kcal/day deficit is the optimal zone: fast enough to see results in 4 weeks, small enough that the body won't break down muscle for energy.

benefits.title: Ideal loss rate
benefits.desc: −400 kcal deficit = ~0.37kg fat/week. More sustainable than crash dieting without exhaustion.

benefits.title: High protein protects muscle
benefits.desc: 2.0g/kg ensures the body prioritizes fat burning instead of muscle breakdown when energy is limited.

benefits.title: Stable blood sugar
benefits.desc: Reduce refined carbs, increase fiber → stable insulin → less new fat accumulation after meals.

benefits.title: Still enough energy to train
benefits.desc: Don't cut too deep — maintain cardio and gym intensity to optimize fat burning.

fat-loss.caution: Don't exceed a 600 kcal/day deficit — high risk of muscle loss, hair loss, and chronic fatigue.
fat-loss.timeframe: 4–8 weeks to see clear results on the scale and in the mirror.

muscle-gain.headline: Quality muscle gain — minimal fat accumulation
muscle-gain.science: A +200–300 kcal/day surplus is 'lean bulk' — enough material to build muscle while limiting excess fat storage.

benefits.title: Effective lean bulk
benefits.desc: +250 kcal light surplus builds muscle gradually and with quality, without rapid fat gain.

benefits.title: Carbs around training
benefits.desc: Load carbs before training (energy) and after training (glycogen recovery) to maximize muscle synthesis.

benefits.title: Muscle grows during sleep
benefits.desc: GH and testosterone peak during deep sleep 7–9h. Sleep deprivation blocks muscle growth.

benefits.title: Progressive overload is key
benefits.desc: Increase load progressively each week alongside sufficient nutrition — without increased load, muscles have no reason to grow.

muscle-gain.caution: Protein should be spread evenly across 4–5 meals/day (20–40g/meal) — more important than eating it all in 1–2 meals.
muscle-gain.timeframe: 8–12 weeks to see clear changes in muscle mass and strength.

endurance.headline: Optimize endurance — long-game performance
endurance.science: Carbohydrates are the priority fuel for cardio activity >60 minutes. Insufficient carbs = cramping, blood sugar crash, early fatigue.

benefits.title: Carbs = speed fuel
benefits.desc: Increase carbs on heavy training days to keep muscle and liver glycogen full before long events.

benefits.title: Electrolytes determine performance
benefits.desc: Sodium + potassium + magnesium keep muscle contractions stable, prevent cramping and maintain endurance.

benefits.title: Protein for cardio recovery
benefits.desc: 1.5g/kg is enough to repair micro-damage to muscle fibers after long cardio without heaviness or slow digestion.

benefits.title: Don't try new foods before race day
benefits.desc: Keep your usual diet 48h before competition — unfamiliar foods can cause digestive disruption.

endurance.caution: Cutting carbs during high-intensity endurance training causes serious fatigue and severe performance decline.
endurance.timeframe: 6–10 weeks to clearly improve endurance and recovery time between sessions.

maintenance.headline: Long-term maintenance — freedom without fear
maintenance.science: The maintenance phase is often overlooked but critically important: it helps the body reset its set point and hormones after a cut or bulk phase.

benefits.title: True stable weight
benefits.desc: Eating around TDEE ±100 kcal helps the body maintain homeostasis and keeps metabolism unrestrained.

benefits.title: No calorie pressure
benefits.desc: 80/20 rule: 80% healthy foods, 20% flexible — enough to sustain long-term without exhaustion.

benefits.title: Periodic check-ins are enough
benefits.desc: Weigh once/week, same time and conditions — just to catch a ±2kg trend and adjust early.

benefits.title: Foundation for the next goal
benefits.desc: Good 8–12 week maintenance creates a stable floor before entering the next cut or bulk phase.

maintenance.caution: Maintenance doesn't mean 'eat anything' — keep core habits: sufficient protein, sufficient veggies, less liquid sugar.
maintenance.timeframe: Maintain at least 8–12 weeks after each cut/bulk phase before starting a new cycle.

tiers_full.keyFact: 80% of results come from the most basic habits — no need to count calories from the start.
tiers_full.detail: The beginner phase focuses on building awareness and healthy eating habits. The goal isn't perfection but consistency.
details: Prioritize protein at every meal: chicken breast, eggs, fish, tofu, yogurt — helps you stay full longer and reduces sugar cravings after meals.
Vegetables in 2/3 of main meals supply micronutrients, fiber, and slow blood sugar absorption.
Water is the foundation: 6–8 glasses/day helps your body metabolize better and reduces confusing thirst for hunger.
At this stage, awareness matters more than counting: knowing which meal lacked protein or had too many carbs is enough.
Cut sugary drinks and ultra-processed snacks — this single change creates the biggest impact with the least effort.
No complex meal plan needed: just ask yourself after every meal — 'Did I get protein? Did I get vegetables?'

tiers_full.keyFact: ½–¼–¼ plate + enough daily protein solves 90% of nutritional needs without a complex tracking app.
tiers_full.detail: The standard phase moves habits from awareness to real structure. You start planning meals, tracking protein, and learning to read nutrition labels.
details: ½–¼–¼ plate: half the plate for veg and protein, a quarter for carbs, a quarter for animal protein — the simplest formula to balance any meal.
Meal prep 1–2 times/week saves 30–60 minutes each day and reduces poor food decisions when hungry (the worst time to decide).
Minimally processed food means choosing ingredients as close to their natural state as possible — steamed chicken breast instead of chicken sausage.
Track protein (~1.6–2g/kg body weight) — the single most important metric: enough protein helps preserve muscle, keeps you full, and aids recovery.
Reading nutrition labels: focus on 3 figures — calories/serving, protein, and the first ingredient listed.
At this stage you begin seeing body changes — this is the time to maintain rather than constantly changing the plan.

tiers_full.keyFact: Personalizing macros to your TDEE and specific goal improves training performance and body composition by 25–40%.
tiers_full.detail: The advanced phase is for those who have built a solid foundation and want to optimize nutrition for a specific goal — fat loss, muscle gain, or performance improvement.
details: Personalized TDEE: instead of using a generic formula, you adjust based on actual body feedback every 2–4 weeks of tracking.
Carb cycling optimizes glycogen: on heavy training days, increase carbs 20–30% for energy; on rest days, cut carbs slightly, increase fat a little for fat burning.
Nutrient timing: 20–30g protein + fast carbs within 30–60 minutes after training improves muscle synthesis and speeds recovery.
Inbody scale once a month provides real data on muscle mass, body fat %, visceral fat — far more accurate than just tracking body weight.
Adjust plan every 4–6 weeks based on data: if body fat hasn't dropped after 4 weeks, cut 100–150 kcal; if losing muscle, increase protein.
At this stage, data-driven consistency and patience matter more than any 'secret' — the body changes over weeks, not days.
